title: Vascular Syndromes of the Forebrain, Brainstem, and Cerebellum
subtitle: Match the deficit pattern to the arterial territory: ICA, AChA, ACA, MCA, PCA, thalamic, vertebrobasilar, border zone and lacunar syndromes

points.text: The ACA supplies the medial surface of the hemisphere and the upper frontal and parietal regions.
points.quote: The ACAs supply the medial surface of the cerebrum and the upper regions of the frontal and parietal lobes

points.text: The MCA covers most of the lateral hemispheric surface plus deep frontal and parietal structures.
points.quote: The MCA supplies most of the lateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere and deep frontal and parietal lobe structures

points.text: The PCA supplies the occipital lobe, the inferior and medial temporal lobe, and parts of the midbrain and thalamus.
points.quote: The PCAs supply the occipital lobes, inferior and medial surface of the temporal lobes, parts of the midbrain and thalamus

points.text: The striatum and thalamus get three groups of perforators: ACA (medial striate), MCA stem (lateral striate) and PCA (posterior striate).
points.quote: medial striate arteries from the proximal ACA; lateral striate arteries from the MCA stem; and posterior striate arteries from the PCAs

points.text: Perforators from the M1 segment of the MCA feed the corona radiata, external capsule, claustrum, putamen, part of the pallidum and the caudate body.
points.quote: Penetrating lenticulostriate arteries supplying the adjacent corona radiata, external capsule, claustrum, putamen, part of the globus pallidus, body of the caudate nucleus

points.text: The AChA feeds the visual pathway at the lateral geniculate/optic tract level and part of the posterior limb of the internal capsule, which explains its triad of hemiparesis, sensory loss and field defect.
points.quote: lateral geniculate body, optic tract, origin of the optic radiations, genu and inferior and medial segments of the posterior limb of the internal capsule

points.text: PICA supplies the inferior vermis and the inferior and posterior cerebellar hemispheres.
points.quote: The PICAs supply the inferior vermis and the inferior and posterior aspects of the cerebellar hemispheres

points.text: AICA supplies the ventral cerebellum, the middle cerebellar peduncle and the caudal pontine tegmentum.
points.quote: The AICAs supply the anterior surface of the simple, superior, and inferior semilunar lobules, flocculus, middle cerebellar peduncle, and caudal pontine tegmentum

points.text: SCA supplies the upper half of the cerebellum, the dentate nuclei and the rostral pontine tegmentum.
points.quote: The SCAs supply the superior half of the cerebellar hemispheres and vermis, dentate nuclei, and rostral pontine tegmentum

points.text: The medulla is fed by the paired vertebral arteries and the unpaired anterior spinal artery.
points.quote: The blood supply to the medulla oblongata arises from the paired VAs and the unpaired anterior spinal artery

points.text: Brainstem blood supply is conceptually divided into four territories.
points.quote: The blood supply to the brainstem is often divided into four distinct territories: anteromedial, anterolateral, lateral, and posterior

points.text: Thalamic infarcts fall into four vascular territories, each with its own syndrome.
points.quote: Thalamic infarctions characteristically involve one of four vascular territories (Fig. 22-4): posterolateral, anterior, paramedian, or dorsal

localizationRules.rule: Amaurosis fugax points to the ICA, not the MCA
localizationRules.explanation: Transient painless monocular visual loss separates an ICA syndrome from an MCA syndrome.
localizationRules.quote: is the hallmark clinical feature that helps distinguish the ICA syndrome from the MCA syndrome

localizationRules.explanation: Both give large hemispheric strokes; reduced alertness and marked leg weakness favor a carotid terminus occlusion.
localizationRules.quote: Decreased level of alertness and severe leg weakness are useful clinical clues to differentiate a carotid T occlusion from a stem of the MCA stroke

localizationRules.rule: Faciolingual hemiparesis localizes to the capsular genu
localizationRules.explanation: Face and tongue weakness, with or without masseter, palatal, pharyngeal, laryngeal or hand weakness, suggests a genu of the internal capsule stroke.
localizationRules.quote: Faciolingual hemiparesis, whether associated with masseter, palatal, pharyngeal, laryngeal, or hand weakness, is highly suggestive of a genu of the internal capsule stroke

localizationRules.rule: Pure sensory stroke: thalamus or pons?
localizationRules.explanation: If both spinothalamic and medial lemniscal modalities are lost, think thalamus, internal capsule or corona radiata; a dissociated loss favors the brainstem (in the pontine form the book describes vibration and position sense impaired with pinprick and temperature preserved).
localizationRules.quote: Conversely, in cases of PSS involving the thalamus, internal capsule, or corona radiata, both spinothalamic and medial lemniscal modalities are compromised

localizationRules.explanation: Leg-predominant weakness with the face spared after hypotension suggests an anterior watershed lesion in the unilateral series the book reviews.
localizationRules.quote: caused crural predominant hemiparesis with facial sparing, at times associated with impaired sensation

keySyndromes.name: Anterior choroidal artery (AChA) syndrome
keySyndromes.clue: The hemianopia may spare the horizontal meridian or appear as quadruple sectoranopias, from optic tract, lateral geniculate or optic radiation involvement; the hemiparesis comes from the posterior limb of the internal capsule.
keySyndromes.quote: infarctions in the AChA territory result in hemiparesis, hemianesthesia, and homonymous hemianopia

keySyndromes.name: ACA syndrome (hemispheric branches)
keySyndromes.triad: Contralateral weakness mainly involving the leg + Abulia + Paratonia (gegenhalten) and grasp reflex
keySyndromes.clue: Bilateral mesiofrontal damage adds frontal release signs, akinetic mutism, paraparesis, urinary incontinence and amnesia with apathy; Heubner-artery infarcts instead give face and arm weakness without sensory loss.
keySyndromes.quote: Involvement of hemispheric ACA branches often results in contralateral weakness mainly involving the leg

keySyndromes.name: MCA superior division syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Contralateral hemiparesis predominantly of upper extremity and face + Hemisensory loss + Conjugate gaze deviation
keySyndromes.clue: Visual fields tend to be preserved; the dominant side gives nonfluent aphasia. Inferior division strokes instead give Wernicke aphasia (left) and hemianopia or quadrantanopia.
keySyndromes.quote: results in contralateral hemiparesis with predominant involvement of the upper extremity and face, hemisensory loss, and conjugate gaze deviation

keySyndromes.name: PCA syndrome (branch occlusion)
keySyndromes.triad: Homonymous hemianopia (striate cortex, optic radiations or lateral geniculate body)
keySyndromes.clue: Macular sparing can be partial or complete if the occipital pole is spared; the defect may be limited to a homonymous quadrantanopia.
keySyndromes.quote: PCA branch occlusion may result in homonymous hemianopia due to infarction of the striate cortex, optic radiations, or lateral geniculate body

keySyndromes.name: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral limb and gait ataxia + Ipsilateral lateropulsion + Ipsilateral facial hypalgesia and thermoanesthesia + Pharyngeal and palatal weakness, dysphagia, dysphonia + Ipsilateral Horner syndrome + Contralateral trunk and extremity hypalgesia and thermoanesthesia
keySyndromes.clue: No limb weakness. Opalski syndrome is the variant with ipsilateral hemiplegia from submedullary extension.
keySyndromes.quote: Wallenberg syndrome results in a constellation of signs and symptoms, including ipsilateral limb and gait ataxia, homolateral lateropulsion

keySyndromes.name: Medial medullary (Dejerine) syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral lower motor neuron weakness of half of the tongue + Contralateral hemiparesis + Loss of position sense and vibration
keySyndromes.clue: The face is often spared, and the ipsilateral tongue paresis is seen in only half of the cases.
keySyndromes.quote: ipsilateral lower motor neuron weakness of half of the tongue and contralateral hemiparesis with associated loss of position sense and vibration

boardTraps.text: Bilateral ACA-MCA border zone ischemia produces bibrachial sensorimotor impairment that the book describes as often confined to the forearms and hands, together with impaired volitional saccades.
boardTraps.quote: Bilateral border zone ischemia between the ACAs and MCAs results in bibrachial cortical sensorimotor impairment often confined to the forearms and hands

boardTraps.text: Leg-predominant weakness is not specific for the ACA: only a minority of such strokes are ACA territory, and the internal capsule, corona radiata or brainstem can be responsible.
boardTraps.quote: ACA territory infarctions account for only one-fourth of all strokes associated with a pattern of leg-predominant weakness

boardTraps.text: Do not rely on a cervical bruit: its absence does not exclude carotid disease because the bruit may vanish with very tight stenosis.
boardTraps.quote: the lack of a cervical bruit has little diagnostic value because the bruit may disappear when the carotid artery stenosis is >90%

boardTraps.text: Babinski-Nageotte is not a synonym for the hemimedullary syndrome; the book defines it as Wallenberg syndrome plus a contralateral hemiplegia.
boardTraps.quote: The eponym Babinski-Nageotte syndrome has been mistakenly used as a synonymous for hemimedullary syndrome

boardTraps.text: A lacunar sensorimotor stroke involves face, arm and leg; selective face and arm involvement with the leg spared points away from a lacune.
boardTraps.quote: Selective involvement of the face and arm, sparing the leg, suggests a non-lacunar mechanism

boardTraps.text: A single transient brainstem symptom is not enough to call a vertebrobasilar TIA.
boardTraps.quote: Transient vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria, or dysphagia by itself is insufficient to establish a diagnosis of vertebrobasilar artery territory transient ischemic attacks
